newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek PM appeals to farmers to lift blockade.
newsitem.headline: Greek PM appeals to farmers to lift blockade.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis appealed to thousands of farmers on Thursday to end a crippling eight-day blockade of road and rail links, saying it was posing a serious threat to the economy.

"The taking over of national roads and paralysing transport are putting an unbearable cost on the economy," said Simitis in his first public comments since the farmers began seizing road and rail links last Thursday.
"The takeovers harm vital interests of other sectors. They violate the rights of our citizens, and endanger the labour and income of other workers," he said in a televised address.
He appealed to farmers, who have blocked land links around Greece with a fleet of 10,000 tractors, to lift their barricades but declined to go beyond veiled threats.
"I appeal to everyone to understand how critical the situation is and to those who have taken over the national road network to free it," he said.
In his first crisis since winning elections in September, he warned that if the farmers' revolt continued it would effect all workers and tax-payers would have to pay more.
"That is why it must stop immediately," he said.
Simitis's is concerned the farmers' uprising will encourage even greater labour unrest in other sectors of the economy.

He held meetings with the two largest labour groupings -- the General Confederation of Greek Workers (GSEE) and civil servants (ADEDY). Their leaders said later they were unmoved and would continue with recent one-day strikes.

Since his 1997 austerity budget last week, Simitis has faced a wave of unrest from teachers, pensioners, students and dock workers. Athens streets reverberate with the chants of various groups protesting his economic policies.
Simitis has said that sacrifices must be made by everyone to meet economic convergence targets with European Union partners and that failure to do so would be a disaster for Greece.
He said the farmers' demands would cost billions of drachma and the government had "nothing more to give".
The farmers want better price supports, cheaper fuel, the rescheduling of $1.3 billion in debts and lower Value Added Tax (VAT) on farmer equipment.

Simitis gave no hint of what he would, or could, do to force the defiant farmers off the roads. Their tractors are now five abreast and stream for kilometres (miles) at more than 40 main junctions around the country.
International and domestic land transport has ground to a halt and queues of stalled lorries stretch along motorways with irate drivers complaining about food, water and sanitation.

The farmers have shut the borders with Bulgaria and Turkey, cut land links between Athens and the second city of Salonika in the north and surrounded Salonika airport, forcing passengers to walk to the terminal.
Sprawling farmers' squatters camps have grown up on the highways, with increasingly sophisticated tents and lodgings.
Farmers watching Simitis on television reacted angrily to his call for an end to their blockade.

"He's very tough on farmers who are fighting for survival but very soft on his policies which led us to this state," said Larissa farmers' leader Yannis Petakis. "Simitis did not make an appeal, he made a threat. But we will continue our struggle."
